einzeiler: Mathematician Jennifer Chayes on how network theory and AI shape our world.
kurzfassung: Mathematician and computer scientist Jennifer Chayes discusses her unconventional path from dropping out of high school to co-founding the field of graphons. She reflects on building interdisciplinary research labs at Microsoft and leading a new college at UC Berkeley. Additionally, she shares her perspectives on the promise and risks of generative artificial intelligence.
stichpunkte: Jennifer Chayes experienced mathematics as a natural way to make sense of the world from early childhood.
She co-founded graphons, a mathematical framework used to understand massive networks without tracking every single entity.
Graphons have found unexpected applications beyond theory, including the interpretation of video content.
As a teenager, Chayes dropped out of high school and lived on the streets of New York City during the early 1970s.
She later returned to education through a dropout school where she ended up teaching the mathematics classes.
At Microsoft, she built interdisciplinary research labs by securing complete scientific freedom rather than focusing on financial compensation.
She views generative AI with a mix of excitement for scientific discovery and caution regarding potential societal harms.
Collaborating with chemists, her team used AI to drastically reduce the time needed to synthesize metal-organic frameworks.

clips.text: The mathematician explains how researchers developed graphons to study the collective properties of infinitely large networks instead of analyzing every single connection.

clips.hook: Living on the streets in the 1970s
clips.text: The guest describes her stormy adolescence, which involved dropping out of high school and spending time on the streets of New York City.
When offered a position at Microsoft, the researcher famously forgot to ask about money or stock options and instead negotiated total autonomy to build interdisciplinary labs.
Artificial intelligence was paired with automated experiments to reduce the time required to synthesize advanced porous materials from three years down to a couple of weeks.

clips.hook: Grabbing the brass ring of opportunity
clips.text: Reflecting on her life, the guest advises listeners to seize unexpected opportunities immediately, even when the timing is far from ideal.

beschreibung:
Much of the code that describes the inner workings of social networks, helps apps predict your musical interests, and underlies innovations in AI traces back to advances in mathematical theory and data science that fundamentally describe how massive networks behave.
Jennifer Chayes helped create that field of math. She also spent 20 years at Microsoft building interdisciplinary research labs. Now, at UC Berkeley, her interests lie in using machine learning to work on topics like materials science, cancer immunotherapy, ethical decision-making, and climate change. She joins Flora for a wide-ranging discussion about math, networks, AI, academia, and her path between them.
Guest:
Dr. Jennifer Chayes is the dean of the College of Computing, Data Science, and Society at UC Berkeley.
